lesson.title: Determinants and volume

lead.text: Start with the simple case from the rubber sheet. A matrix with entries a and d on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere stretches by a across and by d up. The corners (1, 0) and (0, 1) of the tile go to (a, 0) and (0, d), so the 1 m square becomes a rectangle a metres across and d metres up. Its area is a × d.

Every other square on the sheet is stretched the same way, so every area is multiplied by a × d, not only the tile's. A region of 4 m² becomes 4 × a × d. That makes a × d the area factor of the map, the one number that says how many times larger any area becomes.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a map that stretches by 3 across and 4 up. It turns the tile into a rectangle of area 12, so its area factor is 12. The diagonal case is the easy one. For a general matrix the tile does not stay a rectangle, so the next step is to see what shape it becomes and how to measure it.

lead.text: A map stretches every length across by 5 and every length up by 2. It sends a square tile of side 1 m to a rectangle.

reveal.text: The sides become 5 m and 2 m, so the area is 5 × 2 = 10 m². Stretches in separate directions multiply.

lead.text: A general 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d) sends the corner (1, 0) of the tile to (a, c), its first column, and the corner (0, 1) to (b, d), its second column. The square becomes a parallelogram whose sides are those two columns. Take the rows (3, 1) and (2, 2), whose columns are (3, 2) and (1, 2).

Fit the parallelogram inside a rectangle with sides along the axes. Its far corner is (3 + 1, 2 + 2) = (4, 4), so the rectangle is 4 by 4 with area 16. Four kinds of piece lie outside the parallelogram. Two triangles each have area 3 × 2 ÷ 2 = 3, which makes 6. Two more have area 1 × 2 ÷ 2 = 1 each, which makes 2. Two small rectangles are 1 by 2, which makes 4. The parallelogram has area 16 − 6 − 2 − 4 = 4.

afterFigure.text: Doing the same sums with letters in place of numbers leaves ad − bc, which here is 3 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 4. This number is the determinant of the matrix. Take the product of the main diagonal and subtract the product of the other diagonal. When b and c are zero it shrinks to the a × d of the diagonal case.

lead.text: The determinant can be negative. Swap the two rows of the matrix above and its rows become (2, 2) and (3, 1), with determinant 2 × 1 − 2 × 3 = −4. The tile still becomes a parallelogram of area 4, but turned over, as if the rubber sheet had been flipped. The sign records whether the map keeps the tile the right way round or turns it over. The area factor is the size of the determinant with the sign dropped.

Zero is the other special value. Take rows (1, 3) and (2, 6). The second row is double the first. The columns (1, 2) and (3, 6) lie along one line, so the parallelogram has no width. The determinant is 1 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 0, which is the area of a flat shape.
A determinant of zero means the map flattens the whole floor onto a line. Different points then land on the same spot and nothing can send them back, so a map with determinant 0 has no inverse.
The matrix with rows (−2, 0) and (0, 3) flips the direction across and stretches by 2 there. Up it stretches by 3.

reveal.text: You multiplied the two stretches and dropped the sign. The determinant is −6, and its size, 6, is the area factor.

workedSteps.text: Subtract. The area scales by 7, and the sign says the tile is turned over.
Subtract the second from the first. What is the determinant?

lead.text: Swap the two rows of the previous matrix to get rows (1, 3) and (2, 1). Then work out its determinant.

reveal.text: You found the same size with the opposite sign. Swapping rows turns the tile over, and the sign records it.

lead.text: Run a tile through one map and then through another. The first map multiplies its area by the first determinant, and the second map multiplies the result by its own determinant. The two maps together are the matrix product from the earlier lessons, so the product multiplies area by both factors: det(A B) = det A × det B.

Take A with rows (3, 0) and (0, 2), whose determinant is 6, and B with rows (1, 2) and (0, 3), whose determinant is 3. Their product A B has rows (3, 6) and (0, 6), and its determinant is 3 × 6 − 6 × 0 = 18, which is 6 × 3.

The rule also explains why a map with determinant 0 has no inverse. If an inverse existed, doing the map and then its inverse would be the identity, whose determinant is 1. A product with a zero in it cannot equal 1.

In space the same ideas hold with volume in place of area. A diagonal map scales each direction by its own factor, and a cube of side 1 m becomes a box with those three side lengths. Scales of 2 across, 5 up and 3 deep give a box 2 m by 5 m by 3 m, with volume 30 m³.

So a 3 × 3 matrix has a determinant too, and it is the factor for volume. For a diagonal matrix it is the product of the diagonal entries. The sign still records a turn-over, and a zero still means a collapse, now of space onto a plane or a line.
Everything for the 2 × 2 case carries over, though the formula for a general 3 × 3 matrix is longer. The idea stays the same: the determinant is the signed number by which a map multiplies size.
Work with a cube that is 1 m on each side.

lesson.orientation: Read signed area and volume factors and use zero determinant to detect collapse.

blocks.text: The last lesson counted directions: how many independent outputs a matrix has. A matrix does more to the floor than keep or lose directions, because it also stretches it. A good way to see this is to draw a square tile, 1 m by 1 m, on a sheet of stretchy rubber and then pull the sheet.

Pull it three times as far across and five times as far up, and the square becomes a rectangle 3 m by 5 m. Its area has grown from 1 m² to 15 m². Drag one corner sideways instead and the square leans over into a slanted shape whose area is harder to guess. Turn the sheet over and the tile comes back mirror-reversed, with the same area.
This lesson finds one number for each matrix that says how much the map multiplies area by. The number carries a sign, and it turns out to be zero exactly when the map flattens the floor onto a line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate a 2 × 2 determinant and read what it says about area.

recap.keyIdea: A determinant is the signed factor by which a map scales area or volume. Zero means the map collapses space, so there is no inverse.

blocks.text: Back at the rubber sheet, you found that a map multiplies area by its determinant. You calculated a determinant of 5, then −5 after swapping the rows. Dependent columns gave 0, and scale factors multiplied to 24 and 12.

recap.nextHook: Maps can also flatten the floor onto a line, and dropping a point straight onto a line is the simplest case of that. The next lesson finds exactly where a point lands and how much of it is left over.
